title: Praise: the good and the bad
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino argues that quick, generous praise in the classroom can restrict student progress. Prompted by praising her daughter's bike pedalling when it was partly luck and a downhill slope, she reflects on how she has over-praised students in order to make them feel better. She walks through two cases: a disengaged student whose partial answer is called brilliant, and a diligent student whose answer looks right but hides a key misconception. In both, praise gives a false sense of accomplishment that is exposed only when exam marks are lost, and it also demoralises students who really are working hard. She does not dismiss praise, but says it must be tied to genuine work and accurate feedback. Her remedies are to give realistic praise, ask students how they reached an answer, and break the habit of reflexive superlatives. The piece is a personal and practical reflection rather than a research review, and its strength is the concrete scenarios.
points: Over-praising a partial answer tells a student that little thought is needed to do well and reinforces the idea that half-correct work is acceptable.
Praise given to students who are not working hard can disappoint those who are, making effort feel pointless.
Praising an answer that only looks correct can cement a hidden misconception, as in the Student B example.
The author says honest feedback now beats comfort that leads to a shock at exam time.
The three fixes are realistic praise, asking students to talk through their method, and consciously breaking the habit of saying amazing or excellent.
quotes: Letting the student know that their partially correct answer is ‘brilliant’ gives them the message that you don’t need to do much to do well in this subject. There is no thought required

Just as with my daughter and her bike, praise wasn’t very helpful for Student B. They are going to continue working believing they are doing everything right when, in fact, they hold a big misconception. This can cement the misconception in place and make success harder to achieve.

If someone is not working hard, not doing what they are meant to do or incorporating errors in their work but then they still get praised, this provides a false sense of accomplishment that is actually detrimental in the long run.
We cannot expect students to make progress if we are not willing to be realistic with our feedback. Sugar-coating it serves no purpose but to provide a sort of comfort in the short-term.
Usually I find that I over-praise when I am not consciously thinking about what I am saying. Breaking this habit isn’t easy.
